doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Teaching in Philadelphia, commuting to New York, Gravity
summary: He taught in Philadelphia while commuting to New York weekends, met Howard Johnson, jammed, and moved in 1968.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: That’s cool. Well would you say that you made a living as a tuba player for some time before you taught?
No I taught the whole time.

I mean not the whole time, there was a ten year period where I stopped teaching, but I taught, when I left Philadelphia I was teaching. Matter of fact before I left Philadelphia I taught for two years after I finished college. I finished college in ’66 June and I taught from June of ‘66 through ’67, up until June ’68 in Philadelphia. And in ’68 that’s when I came and moved to New York. But through that whole winter of ’67, September through June, I was driving to New York. I would drive, that was when I was working at My Father’s Moustache. And I would drive to New York on Friday night after teaching all week and work at the Moustache Friday and Saturday. And in doing that after a couple of months I met Howard Johnson. Because he was working at My Father’s Moustache, because like I said that was the only gig in town. The other gig was the Red Garter and Dave Bargeron was working at the Red Garter, the trombone player and also a tuba

player, and that was with Blood, Sweat & Tears. He was the tuba player at the Red Garter. And those were the two gigs in town where you could work steady on the tuba. And so I would come in and do the weekend, I met Howard, we would hang out and I started learning how to improvise and stuff and we would, after he finished the gig at 3:30 I would finish at 3:30, and we would meet up at Warren Smith’s loft up on 21st Street and we would hang out and play until four, five, six in the morning and go to sleep and then get up and go have breakfast on the lower east side, you know what I mean? It was a great winter. I learned a bunch. And so I would, by the end of the winter, by say February, he formed the group Gravity.
That is a great name by the way. It’s perfect.

He formed the group Gravity and so not only was I coming in on Friday but I would drive in on Thursday. I wanted to play, you understand? So I would drive that hundred miles from Philadelphia into New York, do a rehearsal after teaching all day on Thursday, get back in my car, drive back to Philadelphia, teach on Friday, get back in my car, drive back to New York and do the weekend in New York. I’m very lucky to be here, I’m telling you, because lots of times I would wake up in a different lane. Yeah. I’m very lucky to be here I’m telling you. I’m going to have to thank somebody because I’m very, very lucky to be here because I mean there’s lots of times I fell asleep when I was driving.
I can imagine after, especially the drive on Friday after the Thursday drive and the Friday teaching.
Right. Friday was the rough one.
Friday was really the rough one. But I did that for like four or five months from January through June and then by July of ’68 I said I’m gone. And I quit my job in Philadelphia and came to New York.
Did you have a family at that time?

No I was just married. I was married but I didn’t have any kids. And I moved to New York and I got a job teaching in New York and I was playing at My Father’s Moustache and doing that, and kept it all going. I would go to rehearsals and that’s when I started going to rehearsals with Sam Rivers, going to rehearsals with Collective Black Artists, so I’d go to two or three rehearsals every week because I was doing the teaching thing that I was doing. So like I said I wanted to play.
